Computational Thinking

Unit 1 • SL

2 Weeks (6 Lessons) • B1.1.1, B1.1.2/3, B1.1.4

Unit Overview

The core of this unit is based on Computational Thinking as a problem-solving toolkit. It focuses on the transition from a "wicked," messy real-world problem to a formalised computational model using abstraction (simplification) and decomposition (breaking down).

What You'll Learn

  • B1.1.1 — Problem specification construction (stakeholders, constraints, inputs/outputs, and success criteria).
  • B1.1.2/3 — The four pillars: Abstraction, Algorithmic Design, Decomposition, and Pattern Recognition. Application to software development, data analysis, and machine learning.
  • B1.1.4 — Flowchart design and tracing using standard symbols.

Key Terminology

Master these terms to succeed in this unit:

Problem Specification Stakeholder Problem Statement Constraints Evaluation Criteria Abstraction Decomposition Pattern Recognition Algorithmic Thinking Flowchart Trace Table Dry Run

Common Misconceptions

  • Decomposition: Students often define this as "breaking down a program." It must be understood as breaking down the problem before any code exists.
  • Abstraction: Misunderstood as "making things complicated." It must be taught as "removing irrelevant detail" to focus on the core logic.
  • Flowcharts: Forgetting to label decision branches (True/False) or leaving flowlines disconnected.

Big Ideas to Consider

  • Knowledge & Maps: "The map is not the territory." How does abstraction change our knowledge of the real world? (e.g., the London Tube Map vs. real geography).
  • Naming as Power: Does naming a problem in a specification "freeze" it into a category that limits our creative solutions?
